teaching.task: # HMS Year 12 V05 (Health in an Australian and global context): cardiovascular disease and cancer. Why has cardiovascular disease mortality fallen while so many Australians still live with it, and how does cancer's story differ? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: Cardiovascular disease means conditions of the heart and blood vessels, like coronary heart disease and stroke. Most of it starts with plaque narrowing the arteries. Its four measures don't move together. Mortality has fallen hugely over decades, though the fall has slowed. Incidence is falling too, mostly from less smoking and better blood pressure control. But prevalence stays high, because people now survive heart attacks and strokes that once killed them. And morbidity has shifted to years of heart failure, or disability after a stroke. Think of a bathtub: new cases pour in, the water is everyone living with it, and deaths drain out. Treatment narrows the drain, so the water stays high. So deaths fall for both reasons: fewer heart attacks happen, and more people survive them. Cancer reads differently. Cancer is many diseases, in which abnormal cells divide without control and can invade other tissue. Mortality is falling, but more slowly. Incidence is rising as a count, mainly because the population is bigger and older, and partly because screening finds cancers once missed. Prevalence is rising strongly, because more are diagnosed and more survive. So more people diagnosed could mean more disease, the same disease found earlier, or more people living long enough to get it. And check for counts against an age-standardised rate, which adjusts for an older population. Counts can rise while that rate falls. One measure is never enough. Picture one disease pathway: exposure to risk, onset, diagnosis, then the outcome. Prevention acts at exposure and onset. Screening acts at diagnosis. Treatment acts at the outcome. Incidence reads onset, so it falls only if prevention works. Mortality reads the outcome, and it falls if prevention or treatment improves, so on its own, it can't tell you which one worked.

scenes.teachingReason: Now the risk factors, sorted two ways. Non-modifiable factors can't be changed: age, sex, family history and inherited genes. Age is the biggest of all, so an ageing population adds cases even if nothing else changes. Modifiable factors can be changed. Heart disease adds high blood pressure, high cholesterol and diabetes. So one prevention effort cuts two of the biggest causes of death at once. And a risk factor raises the chance. It doesn't decide the outcome.

scenes.teachingReason: Where and for whom are they changing? Not evenly. Both follow the income gradient, and improvement has been slower for disadvantaged groups, so some gaps widened. scenes.teachingReason: So, two stories. Cardiovascular disease is, in large part, a prevention story: about half or more of the fall came from fewer people developing it, because policy moves a few big risk factors. Cancer is mostly a detection and treatment story, because it's many diseases. The big exception is lung cancer, where tobacco control worked as it did for the heart. And because cancer gains depend on access, cancer gaps stay stubborn. Yet most spending still goes to treatment, so the case is to shift more toward prevention.
